title: You & Me
hook: The trade alert sounds urgent because it belongs to someone whose clock expires before yours even starts.
counterintuition: The paradox is that advice can be intelligent and still dangerous for you when it was built for another horizon, incentive, and scoreboard.
tryThisNow: Before taking one piece of advice today, write the giver's horizon, incentive, and scoreboard beside your own.
keyTakeaway: Financial signals travel badly unless you first identify your own game: horizon, incentives, income needs, risk, and scoreboard.

breakdown.fastRead:
A phone buzzes with a trade alert beside a retirement account screen. The alert is not necessarily wrong. It may simply belong to a person whose holding period is hours while yours is decades.

You can make a costly mistake by copying a rational move from the wrong game. A trader, retiree, founder, landlord, donor-funded treasurer, and television host can all sound confident while serving different scoreboards. Before you borrow urgency, ask whose incentives created it and whether your horizon can survive it.
breakdown.deepRead:
A grant ledger with colored tabs sits open on a nonprofit treasurer's desk. A tech CFO's note says the organization is holding too much cash. The advice may be smart in a venture-backed company. It may be dangerous when some dollars are restricted, payroll is due Friday, and donor rules decide what cash can actually do.

Advice has an owner, and the owner may be playing for a different prize.

The mechanism is mismatched incentives. People speak from their own time horizon, funding source, risk capacity, and reward system. A developer's cash offer may reveal the buyer's deadline more than the neighborhood's future. A television prediction may be designed for attention, not next year's withdrawals. A competitor's cash-burning plan may make sense under their investor terms and fail under yours. The move is to identify the game before treating the signal as information.

This does not mean ignore everyone. It means translate. Ask what the other person is trying to win, how soon they need to win, what they can afford to lose, and who rewards them for sounding urgent. Then compare that with your own scoreboard.

The limit is isolation. Refusing all outside advice because people differ can become stubbornness. The better habit is filtering, not dismissal.
breakdown.fullRead:
Adrian watches the group chat light up with a day trader's alert while his retirement account sits open in another tab. The trader may be perfectly rational. The problem is that Adrian is about to import the trader's clock, stress, and scoreboard into a plan built for a different life. The alert is information only after he writes his own holding period above it.

Money advice often fails because it sounds universal while being local. It was born inside someone's incentives. A landlord hears a developer's deadline as proof of doom. A retiree hears a television host's urgency and forgets the host is paid for segments, not for her income floor. A founder copies a rival's burn rate without copying the rival's term sheet. A coach copies an academy training plan without copying academy bodies, schedules, or recovery.

Who benefits if you feel urgent right now?

That question is not cynical. It is clarifying. Urgency can be useful when your game demands speed. It can be poisonous when your game demands endurance. Advice can be brilliant for the speaker and expensive for you. The difference is not intelligence. It is fit.

Heidi's purchase offer shows why. The envelope under the rowhouse door looks like information about the neighborhood, and maybe it is. But it is also information about the developer's deadline, financing, and assembly plan. If Heidi sells because the buyer sounds urgent, she may be solving the buyer's clock rather than her own tax bill, rental income, and repair schedule. The offer becomes useful only after the incentive is labeled.

Suzanne faces a cleaner version of the same trap. A tech CFO says her nonprofit holds too much cash, and the advice may be excellent inside a venture-backed company. But restricted grants, payroll dates, and donor rules mean her dollars do not all have the same job. Copying the reserve rule without copying the funding model would turn smart advice into operational risk.

A good filter has three parts. Horizon: when does this move need to work? Incentive: what rewards the person giving the signal? Scoreboard: what counts as success for me? Once those are named, outside advice becomes safer. You can borrow the part that fits and leave the urgency that does not. Translation lets you learn from other games without accidentally joining them.

The counter-objection is that filtering can become an excuse to ignore hard truths. Sometimes another person's game reveals something you need to see. The developer's offer may contain market information. The CFO's reserve critique may expose lazy cash. The trader's alert may highlight real risk. The coach's academy plan may include a useful drill. But each signal still needs translation before action, because the cost of being wrong lands in your game, not theirs.

Do not copy the move until you know the game it came from and the game it will enter.

examples.title: Adrian writes his holding period

planSpec.domain: a long-term saver ignoring a day trader's urgent alert in a group chat
planSpec.audience: an investor whose horizon differs from the loudest voice
planSpec.stakes: copying the trade converts someone else's game into his risk
planSpec.requiredBeat: he writes his holding period above the alert before deciding whether it applies

examples.scenario: You are beside Adrian's phone as a trade alert buzzes in the group chat while his retirement screen shows a target-date fund. The message sounds urgent. His holding period is thirty years. Before tapping sell, Adrian must decide whether to write his own horizon above the alert and ask if the trader's game applies. The written horizon makes the alert belong to someone else's game before Adrian trades away his own.
examples.whatToDo: Write the holding period before acting. Treat the alert as someone else's signal until it matches Adrian's horizon, risk, and purpose.
examples.whyItMatters: The trader may be rational in a short game. Copying that move can import short-game urgency into long-term retirement risk.

examples.title: Heidi asks what deadline the buyer faces

planSpec.domain: a landlord misreading a developer's cash offer as proof the neighborhood is doomed
planSpec.audience: a property owner separating another player's incentives from her own needs
planSpec.stakes: selling in panic may solve the developer's timeline, not hers
planSpec.requiredBeat: she asks what deadline the buyer faces before treating the offer as information

examples.scenario: Which deadline is hidden inside the offer under the rowhouse door? Heidi reads the purchase offer beside her property tax bill while her brother says, "They know something we do not." Heidi must decide whether to treat the price as proof of doom or ask what buyer deadline is pushing the offer. The buyer deadline gives Heidi a second explanation for the offer besides secret knowledge about her home.
examples.whatToDo: Ask about the buyer's deadline and incentives before treating the offer as market truth. Compare their timeline with Heidi's income needs and tax pressure.
examples.whyItMatters: The offer may solve the developer's schedule more than Heidi's problem. A signal from another game must be translated before it becomes evidence.

examples.title: Suzanne marks restricted cash first

planSpec.domain: a nonprofit treasurer resisting advice from a tech CFO about cash reserves
planSpec.audience: a treasurer with donor restrictions and payroll obligations unlike a startup
planSpec.stakes: borrowing the CFO's urgency could endanger restricted funds
planSpec.requiredBeat: she marks which dollars are restricted before applying any outside cash rule

examples.scenario: The grant ledger lies open with colored tabs for restricted funds, payroll date circled in black, and an outside advice note from a tech CFO. Suzanne must decide whether to apply the cash rule immediately or mark which dollars are restricted before deciding whether the startup urgency belongs in a donor-funded organization. The restricted tabs keep Suzanne from importing a startup rule into money that already has promises attached.
examples.whatToDo: Mark restricted cash before applying the outside rule. Use the CFO's advice only after adjusting for donor limits, payroll timing, and nonprofit obligations.
examples.whyItMatters: The same reserve level can mean different things in different games. Borrowing the CFO's urgency without the CFO's incentives can endanger payroll or restricted funds.

examples.title: Marianne writes withdrawals before predictions

planSpec.domain: a retiree filtering financial television through her own income needs
planSpec.audience: a retiree who must distinguish entertainment urgency from spending horizon
planSpec.stakes: acting on someone else's segment could create real bill risk
planSpec.requiredBeat: she writes next year's withdrawals on the notepad before the host's prediction matters

examples.scenario: The financial channel flickers silently above Marianne's handwritten withdrawal schedule. Before, every TV prediction felt like something she had to answer. After writing next year's withdrawals and income floor on the notepad, she must decide whether the host's urgency belongs to her spending horizon or only to the segment. The withdrawal schedule turns the television segment into weather outside the window, not a command inside the plan.
examples.whatToDo: Write the withdrawal schedule before reacting to predictions. Let her income floor decide which signals matter and which are entertainment urgency.
examples.whyItMatters: A television host's horizon is not a retiree's bill schedule. Acting on the wrong urgency can create real income risk.

examples.title: Nathan compares term sheets after the rival fails

planSpec.domain: a founder deciding whether to copy a competitor's cash-burning growth plan
planSpec.audience: a founder whose capital stack and investors are different
planSpec.stakes: copying the competitor may import their incentives without their funding
planSpec.requiredBeat: after a rival implodes, she compares investor terms rather than mocking the strategy

examples.scenario: "They were reckless," a board member says after Nathan lays the rival's press release beside his own investor term sheet and burn-rate table. In the postmortem, Nathan must decide whether to mock the strategy or compare the capital stack that made the rival's game different from his. The term sheet makes Nathan compare games before judging moves that only looked reckless from his side of the table.
examples.whatToDo: Compare investor terms before copying or condemning the burn rate. Ask whether Nathan has the same funding, milestones, and tolerance for failure.
examples.whyItMatters: A cash-burning plan can be rational under one capital stack and fatal under another. The lesson is fit, not moral superiority.

examples.title: Paul maps drills against bus schedules

planSpec.domain: a high school coach declining a training regimen borrowed from an elite academy
planSpec.audience: a coach matching advice to players' bodies, schedules, and goals
planSpec.stakes: copying the regimen could injure students with different constraints
planSpec.requiredBeat: he maps academy practice hours against his players' bus schedules before adopting drills

examples.scenario: It took Paul one season to stop admiring the academy plan as a standalone document. The practice plan sits beside an after-school bus timetable and last year's injury log. He predicts the elite drills will raise standards. Then he maps academy hours against his players' travel constraints and must decide whether the borrowed regimen belongs to his team's game. The bus timetable proves the elite plan is not wrong in general; it is wrong if players cannot live inside it.
examples.whatToDo: Map practice hours, recovery, and bus schedules before adopting drills. Keep only the parts that fit the students' bodies, goals, and constraints.
examples.whyItMatters: Elite advice comes from a different setting. Copying it without the same recovery and schedule can turn ambition into injury.

questions.prompt: A long-term saver sees a day trader's urgent alert in a group chat while his retirement account is built for decades. What should he write before acting?
choices: The trader's latest profit screenshot.
His own holding period and goal.
A promise never to read advice again.
questions.explanation: The holding period identifies the game. The alert may be useful to the trader and irrelevant to retirement money.

questions.prompt: A landlord receives a developer's cash offer under the door and assumes the neighborhood is doomed because the buyer sounds urgent. What should she ask first?
choices: Which neighbor is most afraid.
What deadline and incentive the buyer faces.
How quickly she can panic sell.
questions.explanation: The offer may reflect the buyer's timeline. Understanding incentives prevents another player's urgency from becoming her decision.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit treasurer hears a startup CFO say cash reserves are too high, but her ledger includes restricted grants and Friday payroll. What must be checked before using that advice?
choices: Whether the CFO sounds confident.
Restricted funds, payroll timing, and donor obligations.
Whether startups are always wrong.
questions.explanation: The nonprofit's cash has different constraints. The CFO may be smart but playing a different game.

questions.prompt: A retiree watches a financial host predict urgent action while next year's withdrawals are already planned on a notepad. What filter should she use?
choices: Whether the prediction is dramatic.
The host's tone of voice.
Her income floor and spending horizon.
questions.explanation: Her bills define her game. The host's incentives may be attention, not income stability.

questions.prompt: A founder wants to copy a rival's cash-burning growth plan after a splashy press release, but the rival has different investor terms. What should be compared?
choices: Whether the rival's office looked larger.
Which company sounds bolder.
Capital stack, milestones, and tolerance for failure.
questions.explanation: The same burn rate means different things under different funding terms. Copying the move without the game imports hidden risk.

questions.prompt: A coach copies an elite academy regimen for students who have long bus rides, less recovery, and a different injury history. What is the mistake?
choices: Checking the injury log before adopting drills.
Believing practice can improve players.
Assuming smart advice transfers without matching constraints.
questions.explanation: The academy's game differs in schedule, bodies, and recovery. Advice must be translated before use.

questions.prompt: A person refuses all outside advice because everyone has different incentives, scoreboards, and risk capacity. What is the balanced correction?
choices: Filter advice by horizon and incentives rather than rejecting it all.
Copy the loudest advice immediately.
Only listen to people with identical lives.
questions.explanation: The useful move is translation. Differences do not make advice worthless; they make filtering necessary.

questions.prompt: A market signal comes from someone rewarded for urgency, while your plan rewards patience and steady income. What should you check?
choices: Whether the urgency belongs to their scoreboard or yours.
Whether urgency always means fraud.
Whether patience means ignoring all risk.
questions.explanation: Incentives shape the signal. Urgency can be rational in one game and costly in another.

questions.prompt: Two smart people make opposite financial moves on the same day: one needs cash next month, the other invests for decades. What explains the difference?
choices: Different horizons and scoreboards.
One must be irrational.
Financial decisions cannot be compared at all.
questions.explanation: The same move can fit one horizon and harm another. The point is not no comparison, but comparison after defining the game.

reviewCards.front: A friend sends a trade alert before you act. What three things should you identify?
reviewCards.back: Identify horizon, incentive, and scoreboard: when the move must work, what rewards the signal giver, and what success means for you.

reviewCards.front: A smart person gives advice from a different timeline. Why can smart advice be harmful?
reviewCards.back: It may be smart for a different game. A move built for another person's timeline, risk, or reward system may not transfer.

reviewCards.front: What should a retiree do before acting on a TV prediction?
reviewCards.back: Write the withdrawal schedule and income floor first. Then decide whether the prediction matters to that spending horizon.

reviewCards.front: You do not want to copy blindly or ignore everyone. What does filtering advice avoid?
reviewCards.back: It avoids both blind copying and stubborn isolation. You borrow the part that fits and leave the urgency that belongs to someone else.

reviewCards.front: Why ask who benefits from your urgency?
reviewCards.back: Because urgency often belongs to the signal giver's incentives. If their reward differs from yours, the pressure may not be transferable.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Define your own game before using outside signals. Translate advice through your horizon, incentives, risk capacity, and scoreboard before acting.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an urgent alert reaches me, then I will write my holding period before deciding whether it applies.
If I want to copy a competitor, then I will compare funding, timelines, and downside before copying the move.
If a prediction makes me anxious, then I will check whether the speaker's incentive is attention or my actual outcome.
If someone gives me a rule, then I will ask what game made the rule work for them.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, take one piece of advice you heard and write the giver's horizon, incentive, and scoreboard beside your own.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review one action you almost copied. Ask whether it came from the same game you are playing.

memorableLines.text: Advice has an owner, and the owner may be playing for a different prize.
memorableLines.why: It makes the source of incentives impossible to ignore without dismissing the advice outright.

memorableLines.text: Who benefits if you feel urgent right now?
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a sharp filter for borrowed pressure.

memorableLines.text: Do not copy the move until you know the game it came from and the game it will enter.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the practical rule into a fit test for borrowed advice.
